question: The European Court of Auditors’ special report 01/2026 highlights serious weaknesses in the implementation of olive oil controls. For Greece, it finds that compliance checks were limited to domestically produced olive oil intended for the Greek market, excluding imports and exports. At the same time, sanctioning procedures took 14 months, compared to 1.2 months in Italy.

Gaps in controls and cross-border traceability increase the risk of misrepresentation as to origin and quality, exposing consistent Greek olive producers to unfair competition. Furthermore, the report highlights difficulties in applying uniform sterol limits to varieties such as Koroneiki. In view of the above: 1.

What specific actions will the Commission take, and on what timetable, to close the gaps in Greek controls and promptly impose dissuasive sanctions that take into account the illegal economic benefit?

Does the Commission intend to promote interoperable digital traceability of crossborder movements of olive oil, so as to detect false declarations of Greek origin, without placing a disproportionate burden on small producers?

Will the Commission review, on the basis of scientific data, the sterol limits in order to take into account the natural specificities of Koroneiki, while maintaining effective guarantees against adulteration?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (27.11.2026) The Commission is committed to improving its scrutiny of controls and conformity checks on olive oil. It will provide more detailed guidance on the shortcomings identified by the European Court of Auditors’ (ECA)report, striking an appropriate balance between rigorous controls and administrative burden on national administrations and operators.

The Commission facilitates an exchange of views on actions and sanctions in case of nonconformities between Member States responsible for applying them1. In relation to origin labelling, the Commission considers that the current system guarantees that products placed on the EU market can be traced ‘one-step back/one-step forward’, as required by EU law.

Spain and Italy already have traceability systems and Greece is in the process of putting such a system in place. The Commission will work with Member States on developing and harmonising registers for tracking olive oil movements.

Finally, the Commission has adopted legislation to allow monovarietal extra virgin olive oil from the Koroneiki and Nocellara del Belice varieties to be sold on the EU market when their total sterol content is between 800 and 1000 mg/kg2.
1 See Article 13 of Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2022/2105 of 29 July 2022 laying down rules on

conformity checks of marketing standards for olive oil and methods of analysis of the characteristics of olive oil; OJ L 284, 4.11.2022, p. 23–48; ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg_impl/2022/2105/2022-11-04.

2 Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2026/2358 of 21 August 2026 amending Delegated Regulation (EU) 2022/2104 supplementing Regulation (EU) No 1308/2013 of the European Parliament and of the Council as regards marketing standards for olive oil and Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2026/2342 of 22 October 2026 amending Implementing Regulation (EU) 2022/2105 as regards conformity checks of certain monovarietal extra virgin olive oils; OJ L of 23.
